doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Favorite organists: Jimmy Smith and the turnaround of hearing Larry Young
summary: Levin names Larry Young and Jimmy Smith, and describes seeing Tony Williams' Lifetime with McLaughlin and Young, which changed how he thought about organ.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Right. Who are your favorite organists?
Oh there’s a lot of them. Jimmy Smith — oh I’m blanking. You can edit this right?

Larry Young. Sometimes I get a lot of coffee and I’m racing and racing, and then my thoughts get left — Larry Young is just amazing. There was a big turnaround for me, I think somewhere in the 70s, because I’d been listening to Jimmy Smith, like everybody, and trying to emulate him, which of course you can’t do but it’s fun to try, there’s just so much spirit in his playing. And I went to — I remember the concert but I don’t remember who was headlining it, but John McLaughlin was the opening act. No, Tony Williams —
it was the original, Tony Williams Lifetime. But first — you’re making me think of that stuff.

It was Tony Williams’ Original Lifetime and he had discovered John McLaughlin and John was up there in a cardigan jacket and a tie. He looked like a dork. In fact, nobody knew who he was. And he was playing the most amazing stuff. And it was Tony and John and Larry Young. And Larry was playing a B3 but not through a Leslie, he had this amp, a big guitar amp, it was a Baldwin guitar amp, which I knew because I’d seen it in the music stores, it was a wacky looking thing that nobody was buying, it was I’m sure a big disaster for the company. But that’s what he used. And he was just the exact opposite of what Jimmy was like. He used it to create textures — the organ that is, not the amp — he used the organ to create textures and different sounds. Technically he was a tremendous player but he just was not going the soul groove organ thing at all. And I walked out of there thinking man what have I been doing all these years — just wrong. And I started to track down his stuff. So that was a complete turnaround for me. I still listen to him a lot. It was really tragic that we lost him so soon because I can’t imagine what he’d be doing now.
Right. He was only what in his 30s or something?
Something like that. But he was just doing such incredible stuff. The duos with Elvin Jones and, wow.
